(p-661) Sūrat al-Tawba

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

It has several names: Barā'a (Immunity/Disavowal), al-Tawba (Repentance), al-Muqashqisha (the Purifying), al-Mubaʿthira (the Unveiling), al-Musharrida (the Dispersing), al-Mukhziya (the Humiliating), al-Fāḍiḥa (the Exposing), al-Muthīra (the Stirring Up), al-Ḥāfira (the Digging Out), al-Munakkila (the Punishing), al-Mudamdima (the Annihilating), because in it is the repentance (tawba) of Allah toward the believers; it purifies one from hypocrisy (yuqashqish min al-nifāq), i.e., it clears one of it; it unveils (tubaʿthir) the secrets of the hypocrites, searches for them, stirs them up, digs them out, exposes them, punishes them, disperses them, humiliates them, and destroys them completely (tudamdim ʿalayhim).

As for the omission of the basmala at its beginning, there are several opinions. From ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: that the basmala is a guarantee of safety (amān), and Barā'a was revealed to lift the guarantee of safety. From ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him: that when a sūra or a verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he would say, "Place it in the position where such-and-such is mentioned." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away without explaining to us where to place it. Its story resembled the story of al-Anfāl, because al-Anfāl mentions covenants (ʿuhūd) and Barā'a is about the annulment of covenants (nabdh al-ʿuhūd). Therefore, I joined the two together. Both were called "the Two Companions" (al-qarīnatayn), and they are counted as the seventh of the long sūras (al-ṭiwāl), and they are seven. It was also said: the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ differed. Some said: al-Anfāl and Barā'a are one sūra, revealed concerning fighting. Others said: they are two sūras, so a gap was left between them for the saying of the one who said they are two sūras, and the basmala was omitted for the saying of the one who said they are one sūra.

(p-662) "Barā'a" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is Barā'a" "from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists." The "min" here denotes the starting point of the end (li-ibtidāʾ al-ghāya); it is connected to an omitted verb and is not a relative complement (ṣila), as in your saying: "You have disowned (bari'ta) the religion (min al-dīn)," meaning: this is a disavowal reaching from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants, just as you say: "A letter from so-and-so to so-and-so." Or it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) because it is specified by its description, and the predicate is "to those with whom you made covenants," like your saying: "A man from the Banū Tamīm is in the house." The meaning is that Allah and His Messenger have disowned the covenant that you made with the polytheists, and that it has been thrown back to them (manbūdh ilayhim).

﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾: travel through the land however you wish. As-sayh (touring) means travelling at leisure.

It is narrated that they had made covenants with the polytheists of Makkah and other Arabs, and they broke them, except for some of them, namely the Banu Damrah and the Banu Kinanah. So the covenant was annulled for those who had broken it, and they were ordered to travel through the land for four months, safe wherever they wished, and no one was to harm them. These are the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum), as in His saying: ﴿When the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾ [At-Tawbah: 5]. This was to protect the sacred months from killing and fighting within them. It was revealed in the ninth year after the Hijrah, and the conquest of Makkah was in the eighth year. The commander at that time was 'Attab ibn Usayd.

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed Abu Bakr over the pilgrimage of the ninth year, and then sent 'Ali after him, riding al-'Adba'  (his she-camel), to recite it to the people of the pilgrimage. It was said to him: 'If only you had sent it with Abu Bakr.' He said: 'None may convey it on my behalf except a man from me.' When 'Ali drew near, Abu Bakr heard the sound of the camel and stopped and said: 'This is the sound of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) she-camel.' When he reached him, he said: 'Are you a commander or one commanded?' He said: 'One commanded.' When it was the day before at-Tarwiyah, Abu Bakr gave a sermon and informed them about their rites. On the day of sacrifice, 'Ali stood at Jamrat al-'Aqabah and said: 'O people, I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah to you.' They said: 'With what?' So he recited to them thirty or forty verses, then said: 'I have been commanded with four things: that no polytheist should approach the House after this year, that no one should circumambulate the House naked, that no one should enter Paradise except a believing soul, and that every person with a covenant should have his covenant fulfilled until its term.' Then they said: 'O 'Ali, tell your cousin that we have cast the covenant behind our backs, and there is no covenant between us and him except spear-thrusts and sword-blows.'"

The four months are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram; or twenty days of Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-Awwal and ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. They were sacred (hurum) because they were granted safety during them, and killing and fighting against them was forbidden. Or it is by taghlib (the figure of speech in which one term prevails over another), since Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram are among them.

The majority of scholars hold that fighting is permitted during the sacred months, and that this ruling was abrogated (naskh, the replacement of an earlier ruling by a later one).

﴿And know that you cannot escape Allah﴾: you cannot outrun Him, even if He grants you respite. ﴿And that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾: He will humiliate them in this world through killing, and in the Hereafter through punishment.

﴿وَأذانٌ مِنَ اللهِ ورَسُولِهِ إلى الناسِ﴾ [And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people]. Its grammatical case (irtifa') is like that of بَراءَةٌ (bara'ah, "a disavowal"), on both of the two readings, and the sentence is conjoined (ma'tufah) to a similar sentence before it. The word أذان (adhan) means إيذان (iydhan), which is informing (i'lam), just as أمان (aman) and عطاء ('ata') mean إيمان (iman) and إعطاء (i'ta'), i.e., security and giving. The difference between the first and second sentences is that the first is a report of the establishment of the disavowal, while the second is a report of the obligation to inform people of what has been established. The disavowal is attached to those among the polytheists (mushrikin) who had covenants with the Muslims, whereas the proclamation is attached to "the people" because the disavowal is specific to those bound by treaty and those among them who broke it, while the proclamation is general to all people: those who had a covenant, those who did not, those among the covenant-holders who broke it, and those who did not break it. ﴿يَوْمَ الحَجِّ الأكْبَرِ﴾ [on the day of the greater pilgrimage] refers either to the day of 'Arafah, because standing at 'Arafah is the greatest part of the acts of Hajj, or to the day of sacrifice (al-nahr), because in it the Hajj is completed through the circumambulation (tawaf), the sacrifice, the shaving, and the stoning (ramy). The description of the Hajj as "greater" is because 'Umrah is called "the lesser Hajj."

﴿أنَّ اللهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ [that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists]. That means: بِأنَّ اللهَ (bi-anna Allah), with the complement of the proclamation (silat al-adhan) omitted for brevity. ﴿وَرَسُولِهِ﴾ [and His Messenger] is conjoined either to the implied subject in بَرِيءٌ, or to the inceptive subject (mubtada'), with its predicate omitted, meaning "and His Messenger is free of obligation." It has also been read in the accusative, conjoined to the noun of أنَّ (inna), and in the genitive by attraction (jiwar), or by an oath, like your saying لَعَمْرُكَ (la-'amruka, "by your life"). It is related that a Bedouin heard a man reciting it, and said: "If Allah is free of His Messenger, then I am free of him too." The man seized him by his collar and brought him to 'Umar, and the Bedouin related his recitation. Thereupon 'Umar ordered the teaching of Arabic grammar.

﴿فَإنْ تُبْتُمْ﴾ [So if you repent] from disbelief and treachery,

﴿فَهُوَ﴾ [it] meaning the repentance (p-664) ﴿خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ [is better for you] than persisting in disbelief. ﴿وَإنْ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ﴾ [But if you turn away] from repentance, or persist in turning away and aversion from Islam,

﴿فاعْلَمُوا أنَّكم غَيْرُ مُعْجِزِي اللهِ﴾ [then know that you cannot escape Allah], meaning you cannot outrun Allah, nor escape His seizing and His punishment. ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ [And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment], in place of the good tidings given to the believers, of an everlasting delight.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 4:

﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾ is an exception (istithna') from His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land﴾. The meaning is: ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾; so say to them: "Travel freely," except those among them with whom you made a covenant. ﴿Then they have not failed you in anything﴾ of the conditions of the covenant; that is, they fulfilled the covenant and did not break it. It is also read (lam yanqusukum), meaning "your covenant," and this is more fitting, but the well-known reading is more eloquent, because it is in contrast to "completion" (tamam). ﴿Nor have they supported anyone against you﴾, that is, they did not aid an enemy against you. ﴿Then complete for them their covenant﴾, that is, fulfil it for them fully and completely, ﴿until their term﴾, until the completion of their term. The exception here carries the sense of a transition (istidrak), as if it were said: after you were commanded regarding those who broke their covenants, (but) as for those who did not break them, then complete for them their covenant, and do not treat them as you treat them, and do not make the faithful one equal to the treacherous one. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾. He means: the requirement of piety is that one does not equate the two groups; so fear Allah in this matter.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 5:**

﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾ — i.e., have gone by or come to an end — ﴿the polytheists whom you find, kill them﴾, namely those who broke their covenant with you and aided others against you, ﴿wherever you find them﴾, whether in the sacred territory or outside it, ﴿and seize them﴾ and take them captive. Al-akhdh (seizing) means capturing. ﴿Besiege them﴾ and confine them, and prevent them from moving freely about the lands. ﴿Lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾ — every passage and route through which you watch for them. Its being in the accusative here is as an adverb of place (ẓarf).

﴿But if they repent﴾ from disbelief, ﴿and establish the prayer and give the zakat, then let them go their way﴾ — release them after capture and confinement, or refrain from them and do not molest them. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ by covering over disbelief and treachery against Islam, ﴿Merciful﴾ by lifting the killing before they fulfil the obligations through commitment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 6:

﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾ "Aḥad" (anyone) is in the nominative, governed by a suppressed verb of condition (fi'l shart mudmar) which the apparent verb explains; that is, "And if anyone seeks your protection, [someone] has sought your protection." The meaning is: if one of the polytheists comes to you after the expiry of the months, with no covenant between you and him, and seeks your protection in order to hear what you call to of tawhid and the Qur'an, then grant him protection ﴿until he hears the word of Allah﴾ and reflects upon it, and comes to know the reality of the matter. ﴿Then convey him﴾ after that ﴿to his place of safety﴾, his abode in which he is secure if he does not embrace Islam. Then fight him, if you wish. In this there is evidence that the one granted protection (musta'man) must not be harmed, that he has no right to reside in our land, and that he is to be enabled to return. ﴿That﴾, i.e., the command to grant protection in His words "then grant him protection", ﴿is because they are a people who do not know﴾, because they are an ignorant people who do not know what Islam is, nor what the reality of that to which you call is. Therefore it is necessary to give them security until they hear, or understand the truth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 7:

﴿How can there be for the polytheists a covenant with Allah and with His Messenger?﴾ "Kayfa" (how) is an interrogative used in the sense of disavowal (istinkar), meaning: it is deemed unlikely that a covenant should hold for these people. So do not hope for that, do not entertain it in your souls, and do not think of killing them. Then he qualified this with His words: ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant﴾, meaning: but as for those among them with whom you made a covenant ﴿at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, and whose breach had not become apparent, such as the Banu Kinanah and the Banu Damrah, then await their affair and do not fight them.

﴿So as long as they are upright toward you﴾, meaning: as long as no breach has appeared from them, that is, as long as they remain steadfast in fulfilling the covenant, ﴿be upright toward them﴾ in fulfilling it. "Ma" here is conditional, meaning: if ﴿they are upright toward you, then be upright toward them﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾, meaning: waiting upon them is among the deeds of the righteous.

(p. 666)

How can there be a covenant with them, when, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe regard for kinship or pledge towards you? They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse; and most of them are defiantly disobedient.

Translation of the commentary:

"How (can there be a covenant), when" — the verb is omitted because it is understood; the repetition (of "how") serves to express the improbability of the polytheists remaining steadfast in the covenant. The meaning: how can they have a covenant, and their condition is that "if they gain the upper hand over you" — that is, they prevail over you — after they had reinforced oaths and pacts.

"They do not observe regard for you in kinship or in pledge": "they do not observe" means they do not respect an alliance, nor kinship; "nor pledge" means a covenant. "They please you with their mouths": with the promise of faith and fidelity to the covenant. This is a fresh statement describing their state, in which their outward and inward are at odds, and it confirms the improbability of their steadfastness to the covenant. "But their hearts refuse": faith and fidelity to the covenant. "And most of them are defiantly disobedient": they break the covenant, or they persist stubbornly in disbelief, having neither the manliness that restrains them from lying nor the good disposition that deters them from breaking faith, as is found in some disbelievers in avoiding these two.

ﷺ-free passage; translate faithfully.

"They have bought" means: they exchanged (istabdalu) ﴿the signs of Allah﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an — ﴿for a small price﴾, a meagre worldly gain, namely the following of desires and lusts. ﴿And they have averted [others] from His way﴾: they turned away from it themselves, and turned others away. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they have been doing﴾, that is: wretched is their conduct.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 10:

﴿They do not observe regarding a believer ties of kinship, nor a covenant.﴾ "Wa" (nor) is repeated, because the first (lā) is specific, where He says "fīkum" (regarding you), and the second is general, because He says ﴿regarding a believer﴾. ﴿And those are the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the limit in wrongdoing and wickedness.

﴿But if they repent﴾ from disbelief ﴿and establish the prayer and give the zakat, then they are your brothers﴾, that is, they are your brothers, with the subject elided (fa-hum ikhwanukum) ﴿in religion﴾, not in lineage ﴿And We detail the verses﴾, explaining and clarifying them ﴿for a people who know﴾, who understand, so that they reflect upon them. This is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), as if it were said: whoever reflects upon its details is the one who has knowledge, exhorting toward contemplating what has been detailed of the rulings concerning the covenanted polytheists, and toward preserving them.

(p-667)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 12:

﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant﴾, i.e., they violate the covenants confirmed by oaths, ﴿and attack your religion﴾, and find fault with it, ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾, that is, fight them. He placed ﴿leaders of disbelief﴾ in the place of the pronoun "they," and they were the heads of polytheism, or the chieftains of Quraysh who resolved to expel the Messenger. And they said: if a dhimmi (non-Muslim under protection) attacks the religion of Islam openly, it is permissible to kill him, because the covenant is concluded with him on the condition that he not attack it; so if he attacks it, he has broken his covenant and gone out of the dhimma.

(Leaders) with two hamzas: Kufan and Syrian readers. The rest read it with a single hamza, not lengthened, followed by a kasra-marked ya'. Its original form is: ʾaʾimmatun, because it is the plural of imam, like ʿimad and aʿmida (pillars). The vowel of the first mim was transferred to the unvowelled hamza, and the first mim was assimilated into the second mim. Whoever articulates the two hamzas clearly keeps them in their original form; whoever changes the second into a ya' does so because of its kasra.

﴿Indeed, they have no oaths﴾. He attributed oaths to them in His saying ﴿and if they break their oaths﴾ because He meant the oaths they had displayed; then He said ﴿they have no oaths﴾ in the literal sense. This is evidence for us that the oath of a disbeliever is not an oath. Its meaning according to al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on him, is that they do not fulfil them, because their oath is an oath in his view, since He described it as broken. (No oaths): Syrian reading, meaning: no Islam.

﴿So that they may desist﴾ is connected to ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. That is: let your purpose in fighting them be their cessation from what they are upon after the great offences that have come from them. This is from the utmost of His generosity toward the wrongdoer.

Then he urged them to fight, saying: ﴿Will you not fight against a people who broke their oaths﴾ which they swore in the treaty, ﴿and aimed to expel the Messenger﴾ from Makkah, ﴿and they were the ones who started against you the first time﴾ by fighting. The one who initiates is more unjust, so what prevents you from fighting them?! He reproached them for abandoning the fighting against them and urged them to it. Then he described them with what necessitates urging them to it: breaking the covenant, expelling the Messenger, and initiating the fighting without any justification (p-668) ﴿Do you fear them?﴾ This is a rebuke for their fear of them. ﴿Yet God has more right that you fear Him﴾ by you fearing Him, so fight His enemies. ﴿If you are believers﴾ then fear Him. That is, the requirement of complete faith is that the believer fears none but his Lord and pays no heed to anyone other than Him.

When Allah rebuked them for abandoning fighting, He made the command to fight clear to them by saying: ﴿Fight them﴾, and promised them victory so as to steady their hearts and make their intentions sound, by saying: ﴿Allah will punish them at your hands﴾ by killing, ﴿and disgrace them﴾ by taking them captive, ﴿and give you victory over them﴾, that is, make you prevail over them, ﴿and heal the breasts of a people who believe﴾, a group among them, namely Khuza'ah, the confidants (ʿaybah) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Qur'an 9:15: "And He will remove the rage from their hearts." (That is, for the harm they had suffered at their hands.) God fulfilled all these promises, and this was a proof of the truth of His Prophethood.

"And God turns in forgiveness to whomever He wills" is a new statement, informing that some of the people of Makkah would repent of their disbelief, and that also happened: some of them embraced Islam, such as Abu Sufyan, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and Suhayl ibn Amr. This verse refutes the Mu'tazilah, who say that God willed to turn in forgiveness to all the disbelievers, but they do not repent by their own choice.

"And God is All-Knowing" — He knows what will happen, just as He knows what has already happened. "All-Wise" — in accepting repentance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 16:

﴿Or did you think that you would be left alone while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove (jahadu) and did not take, besides Allah and His Messenger and the believers, any intimate confidant (wali-ja)?﴾ "Am" (أمْ) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the hamzah in it is for reproach concerning the presence of the supposing (al-husban), i.e.: you will not be left in the state you are in until the sincere (al-khullas) among you are distinguished, and they are those who strove in the way of Allah, for the sake of Allah's countenance, ﴿and did not take, besides Allah, nor His Messenger, nor the believers, any intimate confidant (waliyjah)﴾, i.e.: a close companion (bitanah) from among those who oppose the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. "Lamma" (لَمّا): its meaning is expectation (al-tawaqquʿ), and it indicates that the distinguishing of that is expected to occur (mutawaqqaʿun kha'in), and that those who have not made their religion sincerely for Allah, Allah distinguishes them from the sincere ones.

﴿wa-lam yattakhidhu﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) upon ﴿jahadu﴾, falling within the scope of the relative clause (sillah), as if it were said: "while Allah has not yet known the strivers among you and the sincere ones, those who did not take any confidant besides Allah." The intended meaning of the negation of knowledge is the negation of the thing known, like your saying: "Allah does not know from me what was said about me," meaning: "He has not found that in me." The meaning is: Did you think that you would be left without striving and without disavowal of the polytheists? ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ of good or evil, so He will recompense you for it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 17:

﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ it is not right for them, nor is it proper for them, ﴿to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾. (The reading "masjid Allah" in the singular) is transmitted from Makki and Basri readers. It means the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). The plural was used in the (other) reading because it is the qibla of all mosques and their leader (imam), so its maintenance is like the maintenance of all mosques. Also, every spot within it is a mosque. Or the intended sense is the category of mosques. When they are not fit to maintain mosques in general, this covers their not maintaining the Sacred Mosque in particular, which is the foremost of the category and more emphatic. This is because the manner of speech is that of allusion (kinaya), as when you say: "So-and-so does not read the books of Allah," which negates his reading of the Qur'an more strongly than if you stated it directly. ﴿Bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾ by their acknowledgement of worshipping idols. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw in "yaʿmurū" (they maintain). The meaning: it is not proper for them to combine two opposing matters, maintaining the places of worship of Allah while disbelieving in Allah and in His worship. ﴿Those, their deeds have become worthless, and in the Fire they will abide eternally﴾, remaining forever.

﴿Indeed, only those who maintain the mosques of God﴾. Their maintenance (*'imarah*) means: repairing what has fallen into disrepair among them, sweeping them, cleaning them, lighting them with lamps, and protecting them from the things for which mosques were not built, such as worldly talk, because they were built for worship and remembrance (*dhikr*). Among remembrance is the teaching of knowledge (*dars al-'ilm*). ﴿Who believes in God and the Last Day﴾. He did not mention belief in the Messenger, peace be upon him, because it is known that belief in God is accompanied by belief in the Messenger, given that the two are joined in the call to prayer (*adhan*), the call to standing for prayer (*iqamah*), the testimony of faith (*kalimat al-shahadah*), and other things. Or it indicates it by His saying: ﴿and establishes the prayer and gives the zakat﴾. And in His saying ﴿and fears none but God﴾ (p-670) there is an alert to sincerity (*ikhlas*). The intended meaning is fear in matters of religion: that one does not choose the pleasure of anyone other than God over the pleasure of God out of fear of some harm, since the believer may fear dangers and cannot prevent himself from fearing them. It was also said: they used to fear the idols and hope in them, so the intent is to deny that fear from them. ﴿So it is hoped that those will be among the guided﴾. This is a distancing of the polytheists from the positions of guidance and a cutting off of their hopes of benefiting from their deeds, because "'asa" (perhaps/it is hoped) is a word expressing hope. The meaning is: the maintenance of these people alone is upright and is counted as valid by God, not that of anyone else.

﴿Do you consider the providing of water to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah? They are not equal in the sight of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Al-siqaya (the providing of water to the pilgrims) and al-'imara (the maintenance and service of the Sacred Mosque) are both masdar (verbal nouns) derived from saqa and 'amara, like al-siyana and al-wiqaya. There must be an elided annexed noun (mudaf mahdhuf), whose estimate is: "Do you consider the people of the providing of water to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in Allah...?" It has also been said that the masdar here carries the meaning of the active participle (ism al-fa'il). This is confirmed by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr: (سُقاةَ الحاجِّ وعَمَرَةَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ), "the providers of water to the pilgrims and the maintainers of the Sacred Mosque." The meaning is a denunciation of likening the polytheists to the believers, of equating their deeds, which are nullified, with the deeds of the believers, which are established, and of placing them on the same level. Their equating them was considered a wrong added to their wrong of disbelief, because they placed praise and pride in other than their proper place. The verse was revealed in response to the words of al-'Abbas when he was taken captive, when 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) rebuked him for fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and for severing the ties of kinship: "You mention our wrongs and leave out our good deeds?" It was said to him, "Do you have good deeds?" He said, "We maintain the Mosque, we provide water to the pilgrims, and we free the captive." It was also said that al-'Abbas boasted of the providing of water, and Shayba boasted of the maintenance of the Mosque, while 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) boasted of Islam and jihad. So Allah, exalted is He, confirmed 'Ali.

﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives﴾ are ﴿greater in rank with Allah﴾ than the people of al-siqaya (providing water to pilgrims) and al-'imara (maintaining the Sacred Mosque). ﴿And it is they who are the triumphant﴾, not you, who are exclusively entitled to success to the exclusion of them.

(p-671)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 9, verse 21:

﴿Their Lord gives them good news﴾ (*yubashshiruhum*, in Arabic script) is the reading of Hamza.

﴿of mercy from Him, and approval, and gardens﴾. The indefiniteness of *al-mubashshar bihi* (that which the good news is about) is because it comes after the description of the one who describes it. The definiteness of the defined: ﴿for them therein﴾, that is, in the gardens, ﴿is lasting bliss﴾, meaning enduring.
﴿Abiding therein forever. Indeed, Allah has with Him a great reward﴾ — which does not end.

When Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to emigrate (hijrah), a man would say to his son, his brother, and his relatives: "Indeed we have been commanded to emigrate." Some of them would hasten to that and be pleased with it, while others had a wife or child clinging to them, so he would say: "You will leave us with nothing and we will perish," and he would sit with them and abandon the emigration. So the verse was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over belief﴾, meaning: they preferred it and chose it.

﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies﴾, meaning: whoever takes the disbelievers as allies, ﴿then it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 24:

﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, and your clan (ʿashīratukum), your relatives (aqāribukum)﴾ — and (ʿashīrātukum) refers to Abu Bakr — ﴿and the wealth you have acquired (iqtaraftumūhā)﴾, meaning, that which you have earned (iktasabtumūhā), ﴿and the commerce you fear may decline (kasādahā)﴾, meaning, the passing of the time of its brisk trade (nifāqihā),

﴿and dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command﴾ — and this is an immediate punishment, or a delayed retribution, or the conquest of Makkah.

﴿And Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾. The verse rebukes people for the slackness of the bond of religion and the unsteadiness of the rope of certainty that they are in, for you do not find among the most scrupulous of people one whose religion is preferred over fathers, sons, wealth, and worldly enjoyments.

(p-672)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, Allah has given you victory on many battlefields﴾, such as the battle of Badr, Qurayza, al-Nadir, al-Hudaybiyya, Khaybar, and the conquest of Makkah. It is said: the battlefields on which Allah gave victory to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers were eighty. The battlegrounds of war (mawatin al-harb) are its positions (maqamat) and its stations (mawaqif).

﴿And [remember] the day﴾, i.e., "and" remember "the day of Hunayn." Hunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if, where the battle took place between the Muslims, who numbered twelve thousand, and Hawazin and Thaqif, who numbered four thousand. When they met, a man from the Muslims said: "We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers." This displeased the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. ﴿When﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "the day": ﴿your large numbers made you vain⁠﴾. Thus the word of self-admiration at the multitude took hold of the Muslims, and they forgot that Allah is the One who gives victory, not the multitude of troops. So they fled until their scattered band reached Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained alone, steadfast in his position, with none beside him except his uncle al-Abbas, who held the bridle of his mount, and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, his cousin, who held his stirrup. ["He said to al-Abbas: 'Call out to the people,' and al-Abbas, who had a loud voice, cried: 'O companions of the tree!' They gathered, saying: 'Here we are, here we are!' The angels descended, clad in white garments, upon piebald horses. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took a handful of dust and threw it at them, then said: 'They are routed, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!' So they fled." And among his supplications ﷺ that day was: "O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You is the complaint, and You are the One sought for help."] This is the supplication of Musa (peace be upon him) on the day the sea was split.

﴿Yet the earth, vast as it is, became too narrow for you, and you turned back in retreat⁠﴾. "Ma" is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah), and the "ba'" carries the meaning of "with," i.e., "with its vastness," and its reality is that it was accompanied by its vastness, the prepositional phrase being in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as in your saying: "I entered upon him in traveling clothes," meaning, accompanied by them. The meaning is: you found no place to flee to from your enemies, so it was as though the earth had become narrow upon you. ﴿Then you turned back in retreat⁠﴾: then you were routed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 26:

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility﴾ (sakinatahu), that is, His mercy by which they found calm and felt secure, ﴿upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see﴾, meaning: the angels. They were eight thousand, or five thousand, or sixteen thousand. ﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾ by killing, capture, and the taking captive of women and children.

﴿That is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾

"Then Allah will turn in forgiveness to whom He wills after that" ﴿ثُمَّ يَتُوبُ اللهُ مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ عَلى مَن يَشاءُ﴾. They are those among them who embraced Islam. "And Allah is Oft-Forgiving" ﴿واللهُ غَفُورٌ﴾ by covering the disbelief of the enemy with Islam, "Most Merciful" ﴿رَحِيمٌ﴾ by granting victory to the ally after defeat.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 28:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are impure﴾ i.e., possessors of impurity (najas). It is a verbal noun; one says najisa najasan and qadhira qadharan. This is because they carry shirk, which is in the position of impurity (najas), and because they do not purify themselves, do not perform ghusl, and do not avoid impurities. So impurity is attached to them, or they have been made as if they were impurity itself, as an intensification in describing them with it. ﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, meaning, let them not perform Hajj or 'Umrah, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah. ﴿After this year of theirs﴾, which is the year nine after the Hijrah, when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was appointed over the season (al-mawsim, the pilgrimage season). [And the intended meaning of the prohibition of approaching is the prohibition of Hajj and 'Umrah.] This is our school's position: they are not prevented from entering the Haram, the Masjid al-Haram, or all other mosques, according to us. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, they are prevented only from al-Masjid al-Haram specifically. According to Malik, they are prevented from it and from other than it. It has been said that the prohibition of the polytheists from approaching it refers back to the prohibition on the Muslims from enabling them to access it. ﴿And if you fear poverty﴾, i.e., destitution due to the prevention of the polytheists from Hajj, and what you used to gain from their coming to you of benefits and profits.

﴿Then Allah will enrich you from His bounty﴾, from the spoils of war, or from rain and vegetation, or from the trade of the pilgrims of Islam ﴿if He wills﴾. This is an instruction to make matters contingent upon the will of Allah, the Exalted, so that hopes are severed from everything other than Him. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of your circumstances,

﴿All-Wise﴾ in fulfilling your hopes. Or, "All-Knowing" of the interests of the servants, and "All-Wise" in what He decrees and intends.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 29:

It was revealed concerning the People of the Book: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah﴾ because the Jews are dualists (muthanniyya) and the Christians are trinitarians (muthallitha). ﴿Nor in the Last Day﴾ because they hold views about it that contradict what is required, for they claim that there is no eating or drinking in Paradise. ﴿Nor do they forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾ because they do not forbid what has been forbidden in the Book and the Sunnah, or: they do not act upon what is in the Torah and the Gospel,

﴿nor do they adopt the religion of truth﴾, that is, they do not hold to the religion of Islam, which is the truth. It is said: "So-and-so adopts (yadin) such-and-such" when he takes it as his religion and his creed.

﴿from those who were given the Book﴾ is an explanation of "those" (alladhina) preceding it. As for the Magians (majus), they are attached to the People of the Book with regard to the acceptance of the jizya (poll tax), and likewise the Turks, the Indians, and others, unlike the idolaters of the Arabs, on the basis of what al-Zuhri narrated: "The Prophet (ﷺ) made a treaty with the idol-worshippers concerning the jizya, except those who were from the Arabs."

﴿until they give the jizya﴾, that is, until they agree to pay it. It was named jizya because it is something that its people must repay (yajzuna), i.e., discharge (yaqdihi); or it is a recompense for disbelief, given gradually in a manner of humbling. ﴿with willing hand (an yad)﴾, that is, with a compliant hand, not refusing, because whoever refuses and resists does not give his hand, unlike one who submits. Hence they say: "He gave with his hand" when he submitted, and they say: "He withdrew his hand from obedience." Or the meaning is: until they give it "an yad" (from hand to hand), in cash, not on credit, not sent through the hand of anyone, but from the hand of the giver to the hand of the receiver.

﴿while they are humbled (sagharun)﴾, that is, it is taken from them with humiliation and abasement, and this means that one brings it himself, walking and not riding, and hands it over while standing while the collector is seated, and that he is seized roughly and grabbed by his collar and told: "Pay the jizya, O dhimmi!" even if he is paying it, and he is shoved in the back of the neck. It is dropped upon becoming Muslim.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 30:

﴿And the Jews say﴾, all of them or some of them, ﴿"Uzayr is the son of Allah"﴾. It is a subject and predicate, like His saying: ﴿The Messiah is the son of Allah﴾. ʿUzayr is a non-Arabic name (ʿajamiyy), and because of its foreignness and its definiteness it is not declined (imtanaʿa ṣarfuhu). Whoever gives it tanwin, namely ʿAsim and ʿAli, has made it Arabic. ﴿And the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." That is their saying with their mouths﴾, meaning a saying not supported by any proof, nor resting on any clear evidence. It is nothing but a word they utter, empty of any meaning beneath it, like meaningless sounds. ﴿They imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before them﴾. There must be an elision of a genitive noun (mudaf), its estimated form being: "Their saying imitates the saying of them [the earlier ones]." Then the mudaf was elided and the pronoun that was the mudaf ilayhi was put in its place, so it became marfuʿ (nominative). That is: those who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among the Jews and Christians imitate the saying of their predecessors, meaning that this disbelief is ancient among them, not newly invented. Or the pronoun refers to the Christians, meaning: their saying "The Messiah is the son of Allah" imitates the saying of the Jews, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah," because they (the Jews) are older than them. (Yuḍāhiʾūna) is read by ʿAsim. The root of al-muḍāhāh is al-mushābahah (resemblance), and the more common reading omits the hamza. Its derivation is from their saying: imraʾah ḍahyāʾ (a woman with no menses), which is the one who resembles men in that she does not menstruate; so said al-Zajjaj. ﴿May Allah destroy them﴾, meaning: they are deserving that this be said to them.

﴿How are they turned away?﴾ How are they diverted from the truth after the proof has been established?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 31:

﴿They took﴾ — that is, the People of the Book took ﴿their rabbis﴾ (ʿulamāʾahum, their scholars) ﴿and their monks﴾ (nussākahum, their ascetics) ﴿as lords﴾ (arbāban, gods) ﴿besides Allah﴾, in that they obeyed them concerning the making lawful of what Allah had forbidden and the making forbidden of what Allah had made lawful, just as lords are obeyed in their commands and their prohibitions.

﴿And the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ is coordinated with "their rabbis" (ʿaṭf), meaning: they took him as a lord, in that they made him the son of Allah. ﴿Yet they were commanded only to worship one God﴾ — it is permissible to pause here, because what follows is suitable as a new beginning and is also suitable as a description of "one" ﴿there is no god but He; glory be to Him above what they associate﴾ — a declaration of His exaltation above association.

Qur'anic verse: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light, even though the disbelievers hate it.﴾

He likened their state in seeking to nullify the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) by denial to the state of one who wants to blow upon a great light spread across the horizons, while Allah wants to increase it and bring it to the utmost degree of radiance, so that he would extinguish it by his blowing. He used ﴿wa-ya'bā Allāh﴾ ("and Allah refuses") in the sense of "Allah does not want," and therefore it is placed in opposition to "yurīdūn" ("they wish"). Otherwise one does not say "I hated" or "I detested" except with Zayd (as the object).

﴿It is He who sent His Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿with guidance﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and the religion of truth﴾, meaning Islam,

﴿to make it prevail﴾, meaning to make it high and supreme, ﴿over all religion﴾, meaning over the people of all the religions. Or: so that the religion of truth may prevail over every religion ﴿even though the polytheists dislike it﴾.

O you who believe, indeed many of the rabbis (*ahbar*) and monks (*ruhban*) devour the wealth of people in falsehood, ﴿بِالباطِلِ﴾, meaning by bribery (*rishwa*) in judgments. He uses the word "devour" (*akl*) metaphorically for taking.

﴿وَيَصُدُّونَ﴾ and they bar their followers (*saflatahum*) ﴿عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللهِ﴾ from the way of Allah, meaning His religion. ﴿والَّذِينَ يَكْنِزُونَ الذَهَبَ والفِضَّةَ﴾ And those who hoard gold and silver. It is permissible that this refers to the many rabbis and monks, to indicate the combination of two blameworthy traits in them: taking bribes and hoarding wealth, and being stingy with it, withholding it from spending in the way of good. It is also permissible that the reference is to Muslims who hoard and do not spend, and He pairs them with the bribe-takers among the People of the Book as a severe rebuke. (p-٦٧٧) It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whatever its zakat has been paid on is not a hoard (*kanz*), even if it is buried, and whatever has reached the level at which zakat is due but zakat has not been paid on it is a hoard, even if it is visible." Many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, such as ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf and Talha, possessed wealth and managed it, and no one among those who turned away from possession criticized them, because turning away is the choice of the more excellent course, while possessing is permissible and its possessor is not blamed.

﴿وَلا يُنْفِقُونَها في سَبِيلِ اللهِ﴾ and do not spend them in the way of Allah. The pronoun returns to the meaning, because each of the two is dinars and dirhams, so it is like His saying: ﴿وَإنْ طائِفَتانِ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9] ("And if two groups of the believers fight"). Or the pronoun refers to the hoards and wealth. Or its meaning is: "and they do not spend them, nor the gold," just as the meaning of his saying:

*So indeed I and Qayyar are strangers therein*

means: "and Qayyar likewise." The two are singled out for mention from among all other wealth because they are the standard of wealth-holding and the prices of things, and the mention of hoarding them is an indication of what is other than them. ﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ So give them tidings of a painful punishment.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿On the Day when it shall be heated up in the fire of Hell﴾ is that the fire is heated over them, i.e., kindled. He used the masculine verb form (yuhma, "is heated") because it is attributed to the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur, "the prepositional phrase"). Its original form is: "On the day when the fire shall be heated over them." When "the fire" was omitted, it was said "yuhma," because the attribution shifted from the fire to "over them," just as you say: "The story was raised to the emir," and if you do not mention the story, you say: "It was raised to the emir."

﴿And their foreheads, their sides and their backs shall be branded therewith﴾ These parts of the body were singled out because, whenever they saw a poor man, they frowned; and when a gathering brought them together with him, they turned away from him, turned their sides toward him, and presented their backs to him. Or its meaning is: it will be upon the four directions: their fronts, their backs, and their sides.

﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves﴾ It will be said to them: "This is what you hoarded so that your souls would benefit from it, and you did not know that you hoarded it so that your souls would be harmed by it." This is a rebuke.

﴿So taste what you used to hoard﴾ That is: the evil consequence of the wealth which you used to hoard, or the evil consequence of your being hoarders.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾ without any addition. The intended meaning is to show that the rulings of the Sharia (sharʿ) are built upon the lunar months, reckoned by the new moons (ahilla), and not the solar months, ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ in what He established and made obligatory of His wisdom, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh).

﴿On the day He created the heavens and the earth, four of them are sacred﴾: three are consecutive (sard): Dhu al-Qaʿda (dhu al-qaʿda), for sitting out from fighting; Dhu al-Hijja, for the pilgrimage (hajj); and al-Muharram, for the prohibition of fighting in it. And one is single (fard), which is Rajab, because of the Arabs' veneration of it (tarjib), that is, their glorifying of it.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, that is, the straight religion, not what the people of the jahiliyya (jahiliyya) do. The meaning is that the prohibition of the four months is the straight religion and the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, and the Arabs had held fast to it, so they used to glorify these months and prohibit fighting in them, until they introduced the postponement (nasi') and altered it. ﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾, in the sacred months, or in the twelve, ﴿yourselves﴾ by committing sins. ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾: a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the subject (fa'il) or from the object (maf'ul),

﴿as they fight you all together﴾, entirely. ﴿And know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾, that is, He is their helper, urging them to piety by guaranteeing victory to its people.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 37:**

﴿Indeed, the postponement (al-nasi')﴾. With a hamza, it is a verbal noun from *nasa'ahu*, meaning "he postponed it," that is, he delayed it. It means postponing the sanctity of a month to another month. The reason was that they were people of warfare and raids. When the sacred month came and they were engaged in fighting, it was hard for them to give up fighting, so they would make it permissible (*yuhillunahu*) and declare sacred (*yuharrimuna*) another month in its place [p. 679]. Eventually they abandoned restricting the sacred months to their fixed times, so they would declare four months out of the year's months sacred.

﴿An increase in disbelief﴾, that is, this act of theirs is an increase in their disbelief. ﴿By it those who disbelieve are led astray﴾ (*yudallu*) is read by the Kufan reader (*Kufi*), other than Abu Bakr. The pronoun in ﴿they make it lawful one year and make it sacred another year﴾ refers to the postponement. That is, when they made one of the sacred months lawful in one year, they returned and made it sacred in the following year.

﴿So that they may make lawful what Allah has made sacred﴾ means that they may match the count that is the four months and not contradict it. They did contradict the specification, which is one of the two obligations. The lam is connected either to ﴿they make it lawful﴾ and ﴿they make it sacred﴾, or only to "they make it sacred," and this is the apparent meaning. ﴿Then they make lawful what Allah has made sacred﴾, that is, they make lawful, by matching the count alone without specifying particular months, ﴿what Allah has made sacred﴾ of fighting, or of abandoning the specification of the months by their specific identity.

﴿The evil of their deeds has been made attractive to them﴾: Satan made that attractive to them, so they regarded their ugly deeds as good. ﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, while they insist on holding fast to falsehood.

﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter] with you that when it is said to you, "Go forth"﴾ (i.e., "Go out") ﴿in the way of Allah, you grew heavy﴾ ("you grew heavy" is originally *tathaqaltum*, and it is the source form. The *ta'* was assimilated into the following *ta'* (*idgham*, assimilation of consonants), becoming a quiescent *tha'*. The connective *alif* (*alif al-wasl*) was added so that one would not begin with a quiescent letter). That is, you slowed down. ﴿to the earth﴾ (the verb is given the sense of inclining and settling, so it takes *ila*, "to"). That is, you inclined to the world and its desires, and you disliked the hardships and toils of travel. Or, you inclined to remain in your land and your homes. This was at the Battle of Tabuk. They were called to go forth in a time of hardship, drought, and intense heat, with the distance being great and the enemy numerous, so this was difficult for them. It was also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not set out on any campaign without concealing its destination by mentioning something else, except in the Battle of Tabuk, so that the people could prepare the full equipment. ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ (*badal*, "instead of," the Hereafter). ﴿Then the enjoyment of the life of this world, compared to the Hereafter, is but little﴾ (*fi jamb*, "in comparison with," the Hereafter) ﴿except a little.﴾ (p-680)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 39:

﴿Unless you go forth﴾ to the war, ﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all.﴾ This is a severe wrath upon those who are sluggish (al-mutathaqilin), in that He threatens them with an absolute painful punishment that encompasses the punishment of both abodes (the worldly and the Hereafter), and that He will destroy them and replace them with another people better than them and more obedient, and that He is free of need of them in supporting His religion, and their sluggishness does not diminish it in any way. It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿nor will you harm Him﴾ refers to the Messenger, peace be upon him, because Allah promised him that He would protect him from the people and grant him victory, and His promise is certain to occur. ﴿And Allah is over all things﴾ (capable) of replacement, punishment, and other things ﴿Competent.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 40:

﴿Unless you help him﴾ — then Allah will surely help him, just as the one who helped him when there was with him only one man. By His saying, ﴿Allah has already helped him﴾, it indicates that He will help him in the future as He helped him at that time.

﴿When those who disbelieved drove him out﴾ — He attributed the expulsion to the disbelievers because, when they resolved to expel him, Allah permitted him to leave, so it is as if they had driven him out. ﴿The second of two﴾ — one of two, like His saying, ﴿the third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. The two were the Messenger of Allah and Abu Bakr. Its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). ﴿When they were both﴾ — a substitute (badal) for ﴿when He drove him out﴾. ﴿In the cave﴾ — it is a cleft at the top of Thawr, a mountain to the south (yumna) of Makkah at a distance of one hour's journey; they remained in it for three days. ﴿When he said to his companion﴾ — a second substitute — ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾ — with support and protection.

It is said: "The polytheists came up over the cave, and Abu Bakr became apprehensive for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and said: 'If you are struck today, the religion of Allah will perish.' Upon him be blessings and peace, he said: 'What do you think of two whom Allah is the third of?'"

And it is said: When he entered the cave, Allah sent two doves, which laid their eggs at its bottom, and the spider, which spun a web over it. "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'O Allah, blind their eyes.' So they began circling around the cave without perceiving anything, for Allah had taken their sight away from him." They also said: whoever denies the companionship of Abu Bakr has disbelieved, because he denies the words of Allah; and this does not apply to the rest of the Companions.

﴿So Allah sent down His tranquillity﴾ — what He cast into his heart of the security in which he found rest, and He knew that they would not reach him. ﴿Upon him﴾ — upon the Prophet ﷺ, or upon Abu Bakr, because he was fearful, whereas upon him blessings and peace, his heart was tranquil. ﴿And strengthened him with hosts you did not see﴾ — they are the angels, who turned the faces and sight of the disbelievers away from seeing him; or He strengthened him with angels on the day of Badr, al-Ahzab, and Hunayn.

﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved﴾ — that is, their call to disbelief. ﴿The lowest﴾ — ﴿and the word of Allah﴾ — His call to Islam ﴿is the highest﴾. The word "hiya" is a separating pronoun (fasl). ﴿Al-'Ulya﴾. (wa-kalimata Allah) in the accusative: Ya'qub, by coordination; the nominative is on the basis of a new sentence (isti'naf), since it was and has always been高 (exalted).

﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾ — He exalts through His help the people of His word — ﴿Wise﴾ — He humbles the people of polytheism by His wisdom.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 41:

﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ — in going out (al-nufur), eager for it because of your vigour (li-nashatikum lahu), or heavy for it (ʿanhu) because of its hardship upon you. Or: light, because your dependants are few, and heavy, because they are many. Or: light of weapons, and heavy with them. Or: riding and on foot. Or: young and old. Or: lean and fat. Or: healthy and sick.

﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves﴾ — an obligation to strive with both, if possible, or with one of them according to the circumstance and the need, ﴿in the way of Allah. That﴾ — the striving — ﴿is better for you﴾ than abandoning it, ﴿if you know﴾ that this is better; so hasten to it.

It was revealed concerning the hypocrites among those who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk: ﴿If it had been a readily available gain﴾. The *ʿaraḍ* is what presents itself to you of worldly benefits. It is said: "The world is a present commodity (*ʿaraḍ ḥāḍir*), from which both the pious and the wicked eat." That is, if what they were called to had been an easily obtained spoil, ﴿near, and a journey of moderate length﴾, a middling, not too distant trip. *Al-qāṣid* and *al-qaṣd* mean the moderate.

﴿They would have followed you﴾, meaning they would have agreed with you about going out. ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾. *Al-shuqqa* is the distance, the far and arduous journey. ﴿They will swear by God, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you."﴾ This is among the proofs of prophethood, because he informed them of what would happen after the return, and they said just as he had told them. The phrase *bi-Allāh* ("by God") is connected to *sayaḥlifūna* ("they will swear"), or it is part of their own speech, and the word "say" is implied in both readings. That is: "They will swear," meaning those who stayed behind, upon your return from the expedition to Tabuk, offering excuses and saying: ﴿By God, had we been able, we would have gone out with you﴾. Or the reading is ﴿They will swear by God﴾, saying: ﴿Had we been able﴾. His words ﴿we would have gone out﴾ stand in place of the response of the oath (*jawāb al-qasam*, the grammatical answer to the oath), and the *law* ("had") covers all of it. The meaning of *al-istiṭāʿa* ("ability") is either ability in provisions and equipment, or physical ability, as though they were feigning illness.

﴿They destroy themselves﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for *sayaḥlifūna*, or a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) of it, meaning "destroying themselves." The sense is that they destroy themselves by the false oath. Or it is a *ḥāl* of *lakharajnā* ("we would have gone out"), meaning: "we would have gone out with you, even if we destroyed ourselves and cast ourselves into ruin by compelling ourselves to march over that distance." ﴿And God knows that they are surely liars﴾ in what they say.

God pardon you (ʿafā Allāhu ʿanka). This is a metaphorical expression for the lapse (al-zalla), because pardon (al-ʿafw) is a synonym of it. It is one of the gentle forms of reproach (min luṭf al-ʿitāb), by placing the pardon at the beginning of the address. It also indicates his excellence over the rest of the Prophets, peace be upon them, since the like of it is not mentioned for any of the other Prophets, peace be upon them.

Why did you give them permission (limā adhinta lahum)? This explains what was alluded to by the pardon. Its meaning: what was the reason that you gave them permission to remain behind from the campaign when they asked your permission, and offered you their excuses, and why did you not wait before granting permission? "Until those who were truthful become clear to you and you know the liars" (ḥattā yatabayyana lakum alladhīna ṣadaqū wa-taʿlama al-kādhibīna): the truthful one in the excuse becomes clear to you from the liar in it.

It has been said: there were two things which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did, though he had not been commanded to do them: his granting permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the prisoners of war; so God reproached him. This indicates the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, personal judgment) for the Prophets, peace be upon them, because he, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, only did that through ijtihad; and he was reproached although it was permissible for him, because of his leaving what was better (tark al-afḍal), and they are reproached for leaving what is better.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 44:

﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their lives.﴾ It is not the habit of the believers that they ask you permission to strive. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾ This is a promise to them of the greatest reward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 45:

﴿Only those seek your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ means: the hypocrites (munafiqin). They were thirty-nine men.

﴿And their hearts are in doubt﴾ they doubted their religion and were unsettled in their creed. ﴿So in their doubt they waver﴾ they are bewildered, because wavering is the habit of the bewildered, just as steadfastness is the habit of the discerning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 9, verse 46:

﴿And if they had intended to go forth, they would have prepared for it﴾: for the going forth, or for the jihad,

﴿preparation﴾ (*'udda*), meaning equipment (*uhba*), because they were well-off (*mayasir*). Since ﴿And if they had intended to go forth﴾ implies the negation of their going forth and of their readiness for the campaign, it was said: ﴿But Allah disliked their setting out﴾, meaning their rising up to go forth. It is as if it were said: they did not go forth, but they held back from going forth because Allah disliked their setting out. ﴿So He held them back﴾, meaning He made them lazy and weakened their desire to set out. *Tathbit* (holding back) is to stop someone from a matter by making them averse to it. ﴿And it was said: "Sit [remain] with those who sit"﴾: that is, some of them said to others, or the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it in anger at them, or Satan said it by whispering. ﴿With those who sit﴾ is a rebuke to them and a placing of them alongside the women, the children, and the chronically ill, whose habit is to sit in their homes.

(p. 684)

﴿Even if they had gone out among you, they would not have increased you﴾ by their going out with you, ﴿except in corruption﴾, meaning except in corruption and evil. The exception here is connected (*istithna' muttasil*, an exception that is of the same kind as what precedes it), because the meaning is: they would not have added anything to you except corruption. A disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) is one where the excepted item is not of the same kind as the item it is excepted from, as in your saying: "They did not increase you in good except in corruption." In this verse the item from which the exception is made is not mentioned. When it is not mentioned, the exception is made from something general, so it is a connected exception, because corruption is a part of that general thing.

﴿And they would have hurried through your ranks﴾, meaning they would have scurried among you with slander, tale-bearing, and the sowing of discord between people. It is said: *wada'a al-ba'ir wad'an*, meaning the camel hurried, and *awda'tuhu ana*, meaning I made it hurry. The meaning is: they would have driven their mounts quickly among you, and what is intended is hurrying with tale-bearing, because the rider is faster than the one on foot.

In the *mushaf* (the written copy of the Qur'an) it is written ﴿*wa-la-awda'u*﴾ with an added *alif*. This is because the *fathah* (the short vowel mark) was written as an *alif* before the Arabic script (*al-khatt al-'arabi*) was developed, and the Arabic script was invented shortly before the revelation of the Qur'an. A trace of that *alif* remained in the habits of writing, so they wrote the form of the *hamzah* as an *alif* and its *fathah* as another *alif*. A similar case is ﴿*or I will surely slaughter him*﴾ [An-Naml: 21].

﴿Seeking to cause you trouble﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the pronoun in *awda'u*. Meaning: they seek to tempt you by causing discord among you and by corrupting your intentions in your military campaign.

﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾, meaning tale-bearers who listen to your conversation and then carry it to them. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning of the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, they had sought discord﴾ by turning people away, or by plotting to assassinate him, peace and blessings be upon him, on the night of al-ʿAqaba, or by returning to (the disbelief of) the day of Uhud ﴿before⁠﴾, that is, before the expedition of Tabuk, ﴿and they upended matters for you﴾, meaning they devised schemes and stratagems against you and deliberated opinions on how to nullify your affair ﴿until the truth came﴾, and this is Your support and victory.

﴿And the command of Allah prevailed﴾, and His religion overcame, and His law became supreme ﴿while they were averse﴾, meaning: in spite of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 49:

﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave and do not put me to trial."﴾ That is, do not put me into fitnah (trial, i.e., sin) by not granting me leave; for if I remain behind without your permission, I will have sinned. Or, "Do not cast me into ruin," for if I go out with you, my wealth and my dependents will be destroyed. It is said: al-Jadd ibn Qays, the hypocrite, said: "The Ansar already know that I am greatly drawn to women, so do not put me to trial with the daughters of Banu al-Asfar," meaning the women of the Romans. "But I will help you with my wealth, so leave me." ﴿Certainly, into trial they have fallen﴾ meaning: the fitnah is the very thing into which they have fallen, namely the fitnah of remaining behind.

﴿And indeed, Hell is encompassing of the disbelievers﴾ now, because the causes of encompassing are already with them; or it will encompass them on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 50:

﴿If good befalls you﴾ in some of the military expeditions, ﴿a good thing﴾, i.e. victory and booty,

﴿it grieves them; and if a misfortune befalls you﴾, i.e. a calamity and hardship in some of its forms, like what happened on the Day of Uhud,

﴿they say, "We had already taken our precaution"﴾, i.e. the matter we are characterized by, of caution, vigilance, and acting with resolve,

﴿before,﴾ i.e. before what happened, ﴿and they turn away﴾ from the place of speaking about that, back to their families, ﴿rejoicing﴾, i.e. delighted.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 51:

﴿Say: Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has decreed for us.﴾ That is: what He has decreed of good or of evil. ﴿He is our Protector (mawla),﴾ that is, the One who takes charge of us, and we take Him as our Protector. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ And it is the right of the believers that they not place their reliance (tawakkul) on anyone other than Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 52:

﴿Say: "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best outcomes?"﴾ (tarabbasun: you wait, expect) "tanthurun" means you wait for us. ﴿Anything but one of the two best outcomes﴾, namely victory or martyrdom. ﴿And we await for you﴾ one of the two worst outcomes: either ﴿that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself﴾, which is a calamity from the sky, as came upon ʿAd and Thamud; "or" with a punishment ﴿at our hands﴾, which is killing for disbelief.

﴿So wait﴾ for us for what we have mentioned, ﴿indeed we are waiting along with you﴾ for what your end will be.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 53:

﴿Say: "Spend [in charity], willingly or unwillingly"﴾ in the ways of righteousness. [The words] ﴿willingly﴾ [i.e.] complying, "or unwillingly" [i.e.] compelled, are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl). (Kurhan, "unwillingly") is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī. It is an imperative in the sense of a statement, and its meaning is: ﴿It will not be accepted from you﴾ whether you spend willingly or unwillingly. Similar to it is ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80]. And the poet's saying:

Treat us harshly or treat us kindly, you will not be blamed by us,
nor will you be despised by us, should you turn away.

That is: Allah will not forgive them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; and we will not blame you whether you harm us or do good to us. The reverse of this has also been permitted in your saying: "May Allah have mercy on Zayd." The meaning of non-acceptance is that the Prophet (ﷺ) returns it to them and does not accept it, or Allah does not reward it. His saying "willingly" means: without compulsion from Allah and His Messenger. And "unwillingly" means: compelled. Compulsion is called "ikrah" (coercion) because they were hypocrites, so their being obligated to spend was burdensome to them, like coercion. ﴿Indeed you﴾ is the causal explanation for the rejection of their spending. ﴿Were a defiantly disobedient people﴾, rebellious and transgressing.

And with the *yāʾ* (*bi-l-yāʾ*, meaning the verb is read as *yuqbala* with a *yāʾ* in place of *tāʾ*, so the verb is third-person): Ḥamzah and ʿAlī.

﴿Nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them﴾. "Anna-hum" is the *fāʿil* (subject, the doer of the verb) of *manaʿa* (prevented), while "hum" and "an tuqbila" (that it be accepted) are its two objects (*mafʿūlān*, the two direct objects of the verb). The meaning is: nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except their disbelief ﴿in God and His Messenger﴾. ﴿And they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy﴾, the plural of *kaslān* (lazy), ﴿and they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾, because they do not intend by these two acts the countenance of God, exalted is He. He described them as giving "willingly" in His saying ﴿willingly﴾, and He negated that willingness here, because what is meant by their willingness is that they spend without compulsion from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or from their leaders. Their giving in that manner is only out of dislike and necessity, not out of desire and choice.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 55:

﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world﴾. Al-i'jab (being impressed) with something means that you are pleased with it, delighted by it, admiring of its beauty. The meaning is: (p-687) do not find pleasing what they have been given of the adornment of this world, for Allah has given them what He gave them only to punish them through its calamities, or through spending from it in matters of good while they dislike doing so, or through the plundering of their wealth and the taking captive of their children, or through gathering it, guarding it, loving it, being stingy with it, and fearing for it. All of this is punishment.

﴿And their souls depart while they are disbelievers﴾. That is, their spirits leave their bodies. The root of zuhuq (departure) is leaving with difficulty. The verse indicates the invalidity of the view that it is required (for Allah) to do what is best (al-aslah), because it informs that giving them wealth and children is for punishment and for their remaining upon disbelief, and upon Allah's willing acts of disobedience, since willing the punishment is willing that for which one is punished; and likewise willing that they die upon disbelief.

They swear by God that they are truly of you, [meaning] of the body of the Muslims, "and they are not of you, but they are a people who are afraid (yafraqun)." They fear being killed, and what is done to the polytheists, so they feign Islam out of taqiyya (dissimulation for self-protection).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 57:

﴿Had they found a refuge﴾, a place to which they could retreat and fortify themselves, [such as] a mountaintop, a fortress, or an island.

﴿Or caves﴾, or ravines, ﴿or a hideaway﴾, or a tunnel into which they could slip away. It is a form of the verbal noun (ism mufta'al) derived from "al-dukhul" (entering). ﴿They would have turned towards it﴾, meaning they would have hurried toward it, ﴿rushing headlong﴾, meaning they would have hastened with a speed that nothing could check, like a runaway horse (min al-faras al-jumuh).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 58:**

﴿And among them﴾ [are some] of the hypocrites ﴿who find fault with you concerning the alms (sadaqat)﴾, that is, who criticize you regarding the distribution of the alms and speak against you,

﴿If they are given from them, they are satisfied; and if they are not given from them, behold, they become angry﴾. "Idha" (إذا) here is for the sudden occurrence (lil-mufajah), meaning: and if they are not given from them, they suddenly become angry. He described them as being pleased and angered for their own sake and not for the sake of religion or what benefits its people, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was winning over the hearts of the people of Makkah on that day by lavishing the spoils upon them, so the hypocrites became vexed at him.

(p-688)

It must be translated faithfully. Here is the translation:

The answer to "law" (if) is omitted; its implied meaning is: ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾ it would have been better for them. The meaning is: ﴿And if only they had been content﴾ with what the Messenger gave them of the spoils, and their souls were pleased with it, even if their share was small. "And said": ﴿Allah is sufficient for us﴾ — the bounty and provision of Allah suffice us, and "sufficient for us" is what has been apportioned to us. ﴿Allah will soon give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger﴾ — He will grant us another spoil, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will give us more than what he has given us today. ﴿Indeed, to Allah we are turning in hope﴾ — that He will make us gain His bounty. "Indeed, to Allah we are turning in hope." Then he explained the places where the alms (sadaqat, i.e., zakat) are to be placed, saying:

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 60:**

﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy﴾. This is a restriction (*qasr*, exclusive limitation) of the category of charity to the enumerated groups. That is, charity is specifically for them and does not go beyond them to others. It is as if it were said: "It is for them only, and not for anyone else," like your saying: "The caliphate is only for Quraysh," meaning that it does not pass beyond them and is not for anyone other than them. It is possible that it be spent on all the categories, and it is possible that it be spent on some of them, as is our school's view. It is related from Hudhayfah, Ibn Abbas, and others among the Companions and the Successors that they said: "Whichever category you place it in, it suffices you." According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, it must be spent on the categories. This is also related from Ikrimah. Then, the *faqir* (poor person) is the one who does not ask, because he has what suffices him for the present. The *miskin* (needy person) is the one who asks, because he finds nothing, so he is in a weaker condition than the *faqir*. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, it is the reverse.

﴿and those employed to collect it﴾: they are the collectors who receive it. ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾ to Islam: nobles of the Arabs whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would win over so that they would embrace Islam, and a group of them who had embraced Islam, whom he would give in order to confirm them in Islam. ﴿and for the freeing of captives﴾: these are the *mukatabun* (slaves contracted to purchase their own freedom), who are assisted from it. ﴿and those in debt﴾: those who are overwhelmed by debts. ﴿and in the cause of God﴾: the poor among the warriors, or the pilgrims who have been cut off from their means. ﴿and the wayfarer﴾: the traveler who has been cut off from his wealth. He shifted from the preposition *li-* (for) to *fi* (in) in the last four categories, to indicate that they are more firmly entitled to receive charity than those mentioned before them, because *fi* denotes a container, so it draws attention to the fact that they are worthy of having charity placed in them and of being made its recipients. The repetition of *fi* in ﴿and in the cause of God and the wayfarer﴾ indicates a distinction and preference for these two over the captives and the debtors. This verse came amid the mention of the hypocrites in order to show, by the restriction of charity to these categories exclusively and to the exclusion of others, that the hypocrites are not among them, to cut off their greed and to indicate that they are distant from it and from its recipients. What have they to do with it, and what authority did they have to speak about it or to criticize the one who distributes it? The share of those whose hearts are to be reconciled fell away by the consensus (*ijma'*) of the Companions at the beginning of the caliphate of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, because God strengthened Islam and made them unnecessary. A ruling, once it is established as rationally grounded on a particular cause, ceases and ends when that cause is removed.

﴿as an obligation from God﴾: this is in the sense of an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar*), because His saying ﴿charity is only for the poor﴾ means: God has made charity obligatory for them. ﴿And God is All-Knowing﴾ of what is in the public interest, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in the distribution.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 9, verse 61:

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is an ear."﴾ Al-udhun (an ear, i.e., one who is credulous): the man who believes everything he hears and accepts the word of everyone. It is named after the organ of hearing, as if his whole being were a listening ear. Their harming him was their saying about him, "He is an ear." They intended by it blame, and that he is one of those who have simple hearts and are easily deceived. So Allah the Exalted interpreted it as something that is praise for him and commendation of him, and said: ﴿Say: "An ear of good for you."﴾ It is like your saying "a man of truth," meaning excellence and righteousness. It is as if it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what an excellent ear!" It is also permissible that it means: he is an ear for good and truth, and for what must be heard and accepted, and he is not an ear for anything other than that. Then He explained his being ﴿an ear of good﴾ by saying that he ﴿believes in Allah﴾, i.e., he gives credence to what evidence has established for him, ﴿and believes the believers﴾, and accepts from the sincere believers among the Emigrants and the Helpers. The verb of belief was transitive with the preposition bi (in) toward Allah, because what is intended by it is affirmation of Allah, which is the opposite of disbelieving in Him, and toward the believers with the preposition li (to/for), because what is intended is listening to the believers and submitting to them what they say and accepting it, since they are truthful in his sight. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And you would not be a believer to us﴾ [Yusuf: 17], how it departs from bi? ﴿And a mercy﴾ by conjunction with (p-690) "an ear." (And a mercy): Hamzah reads it in the genitive, as a conjunction with "of good," meaning: he is an ear of good and an ear of mercy, who hears nothing but these two and does not accept anything else. ﴿For those of you who believe﴾, i.e., "and" he is "a mercy for those of you who believe," meaning: you hypocrites who display faith, since he accepts your outward faith and does not expose your secrets and does not treat you as he treats the polytheists.
